title: We Need to Help Our Kids Learn Perspective
author: Shari Keller
summary: Shari Keller uses a homeschool debate over pink plastic flamingos to argue that debate belongs at the core of a curriculum. Her kids had to argue positions they might not hold, which forced them to imagine the viewpoint of someone who would want the flamingos, and the point of the exercise was perspective rather than a right answer. The rules required listening before responding, checking whether online facts came from reliable sources, and resisting the urge to shout down or cancel an opponent. She frames the aim as raising adults who can listen, question supposed facts, and empathise with people who disagree. Her practical advice is to start with silly questions so children practise taking another person's view.
points: Debating assigned positions trains students to take another person's perspective, which is the real aim rather than winning.
Rules that require listening first and responding to the other side's actual point teach students to engage with uncomfortable views.
Pausing to judge whether a source is reliable enough to build an argument on turns debate into practice in evaluating facts.
Starting with low-stakes silly topics such as lawn flamingos lets children build the skill before tackling consequential questions.
quotes: Overall it was one of the most fun debates we had, partly for its silliness, but also for the fact that our kids really put themselves in the mindset of who they imagined would want the flamingos in their front lawn, and why.

During any given debate, we often paused (kids and parents alike) to look up ‘facts’ online and decide if the source of information was one they thought ‘reliable’ enough to use to compose an argument.

As part of the rules of debate, kid 1 had to listen first, then respond to the point kid 2 was making. They couldn’t just get mad, yell, or ‘cancel’ the other person. They had to pay attention to even uncomfortable points of view and consider them in order to win a debate.

Did things get heated? Yeah, definitely. Did our kids get creative with their arguments? Yep, often in loo of ‘facts’ they learned to resort to persuasive reasoning techniques. They learned to highlight and ‘manage’ information to win a debate and get the other person to see something in a new light. Not unlike real life.

The simple answer is: kids need to develop critical thinking skills. They need to be able to think about, and talk about, something — a given piece of information, a ‘fact,’ a situation in the world — from different points of view and make the effort to become informed about various perspectives on that topic.

They need to become adults who will question ‘facts’ and do their own research, who will make an effort to see beyond their own social or political views, who will talk with people who may not share their views, and who will have empathy for people who sit on the other side of the fence, or who simply have a different perspective.
It is easy to forget how to listen, how to empathize, how to speak respectfully, and how to work constructively with each other to maintain a constructive society.
